derives_from: **`kn__kn-IN.json`**, by a character shift rather than a rewrite: Malayalam’s codepoints are Kannada’s + 0x80 exactly, both blocks being ISCII-ordered, and every character that table emits shifts to an assigned Malayalam codepoint of the same Unicode name — checked against `unicodedata`, with an assertion in `tmp/ml/build_respell.py` that raises on the first one that does not. Kannada’s own derivation from Telugu had the same property one step back; Telugu’s from Hindi hit two unassigned codepoints and had to override them by hand. The two scripts also share the whole mechanism the table is about — a consonant letter that already says [a], so three spellings per consonant and `spellSlot` choosing on what the syllable has already emitted — and, unlike Devanagari, both write every vowel they pronounce, neither deletes the word-final inherent one, and neither has a nukta. **Gundert’s *A Malayalam and English Dictionary* (Basel Mission, 1872) on DSAL and Asher & Kumari’s *Malayalam* (Routledge Descriptive Grammars, 1997)** fix which letter an educated Malayalam reader expects for a foreign sound: ഫ for /f/, ജ for /z/, no nukta anywhere. `content/RESPELL-SYSTEMS.md` names no Malayalam pronunciation key and no published one was found — Malayalam lexicography prints no respelling column, because the orthography is shallow enough not to need one, which is what Gujarati’s, Kannada’s and Czech’s entries also say — so what is adapted is stated here rather than cited. The loanword spellings that decide the hard cases are Malayalam’s own and are checkable on any newspaper page: ഫോൺ, ബാങ്ക്, പ്ലാറ്റ്ഫോം, ഡോക്ടർ, എടിഎം, വൈ-ഫൈ, ആംബുലൻസ്.

deviations.rule: Kannada’s coda `C + ್`, on the five consonants Malayalam has a chillu for
deviations.why: **Replaced with the chillu letters ൺ ൻ ർ ൽ ൾ, and this is the one change that makes the output read as Malayalam rather than as Kannada transliterated.** A chillu is a standalone codepoint for exactly what a `coda` rule emits — a consonant with its own inherent vowel killed — and modern Malayalam writes it in both the positions a coda occupies: word-finally (അവൻ, അവർ, പാൽ, ആൾ, കൺ) and before a following consonant that does not fuse with it (ആംബുലൻസ്, വർക്ക്, ആൾക്കാർ). It also disposes of a shaping risk for free, since a chillu carries no virama at all. **The four English `-er` nuclei `ɚ ɝ ɜ ɜː` move with it**, because their whole spelling is a consonant plus a virama: `അർ` and `ർ`, which is how Malayalam already writes those very words — ഡോക്ടർ, കമ്പ്യൂട്ടർ, നമ്പർ. A geminate is left alone: `ന്ന്` is the nna conjunct with a chandrakkala and stays one, guarded on what precedes the letter rather than on the letter itself.

Becomes ള, Malayalam’s own retroflex lateral, and its coda becomes ൾ. ള is an everyday letter — മലയാളം, വെള്ളം, ആൾ — and the six packs that carry `ɭ` besides Russian (`ta te kn gu mr` and `ml` itself, 1,240 cells between them) all have a real retroflex lateral, which Malayalam print writes with ള: തമിഴ്, വേളാങ്കണ്ണി. The cost is Russian’s hard л, 436 cells, which is velarised rather than retroflex — and of the two letters Malayalam has, ള is the dark one, so it is the closer approximation of the two rather than a worse one than ല.

Becomes ഴ. Malayalam ഴ **is** [ɻ]; Tamil’s ழ is the same letter and the same sound (100 cells), Malayalam’s own column has 72, and Mandarin’s r- is analysed as [ɻ] too (27). Kannada maps it to ರ and throws the distinction away, having no letter for it. No chillu is used: ൖ U+0D56 exists and is archaic, so a coda ഴ keeps its chandrakkala — തമിഴ് is what Malayalam writes.

deviations.rule: The two rhotics, which Malayalam contrasts and this table deliberately does not
deviations.why: **Malayalam writes ര [ɾ] against റ [r] and the pair is phonemic** — കര *shore* against കറ *stain*, and espeak’s `ml` voice distinguishes them correctly, which no other Dravidian voice here does. Mapping `ɾ`->ര and `r`->റ is nevertheless refused, on a fact about the corpus rather than about Malayalam: **this corpus’s `r`/`ɾ` split is not a trill/tap split.** Telugu’s ర, Kannada’s ರ and Tamil’s ர are taps written `r` (567 + 552 + 402 cells), Bengali’s, Hindi’s, Gujarati’s and Marathi’s identical taps are written `ɾ`, Indonesian’s tap is `r` and Italian’s trill is `r` too. Conditioning on the symbol would give റ to ರ and ര to र — backwards for two cognate letters — on well over a thousand cells. So every rhotic takes ര, which is Kannada’s answer, and റ appears only in this pack’s own `text`.

deviations.rule: Kannada’s `ʂ` -> ಶ, which contradicts its own note
deviations.why: Becomes ഷ. **This repairs a documentation-against-data mismatch in the table this derives from**, reported for `kn` rather than edited there, which is the precedent tmp/punjabi.md set: Kannada’s `approximations` field says "/ʂ ʈʂ ʈʂʰ/ keep ಷ ಚ ಛ, since Kannada ಷ is a live letter with its own retroflex value rather than Hindi’s ष" — and its table maps `ʂ` to **ಶ**, with ಷ emitted by no rule at all. Malayalam ഷ is [ʂ] and is an everyday letter (ഭാഷ, പുരുഷൻ, ഇഷ്ടം, ഷോപ്പ്), so this table keeps `ʃ` (ശ) and `ʂ` (ഷ) apart, which the script writes and which Mandarin’s sh-, Swedish’s sj- and the Sanskrit layer of `hi te kn gu mr ne ta` all want. `ʈʂ` and `ʈʂʰ` keep ച and ഛ, as inherited.

Written ൗ U+0D57 throughout. Both codepoints encode the same sign; ൗ is what every Kerala newspaper, textbook and street sign has used since the 1971 reform and what this pack’s own `text` writes (ശൗചാലയം, സൗജന്യം, പൗണ്ട്), so keeping ൌ would have the two columns disagree on one sign.

deviations.rule: Kannada’s two nasal fixups, and one of Malayalam’s own
deviations.why: The two inherited ones move with the chillu — a syllable-internal coda /n/ now emits ൻ, so the pattern that turns it into the anusvara before a stop matches the chillu. **The third is Malayalam’s own and it is not optional: a word-final /m/ is written ം, never മ്**, in every Malayalam word native or borrowed (മലയാളം, റൂം, ടീം, ആൽബം). Without it *room* would print റൂമ്, which a Malayalam reader reads with a samvrutokaram the English word does not have.

deviations.rule: Kannada’s repair of Telugu’s `r̝` — Czech’s ř
deviations.why: Carried over unchanged: `r̝` has the same four rules `r` has, so Czech `přes` prints പ്രെസ് rather than the *pa-res* Telugu’s stray `onset` rule produces. Eight rows of the Czech pack reach it. Reported for `te` rather than edited there, which is the precedent tmp/punjabi.md set.

deviations.rule: Hindi’s word-final virama strip, which Telugu and Kannada both deleted
deviations.why: Stays deleted, and Malayalam is the strongest case of the three. Every vowel Malayalam pronounces is written, and a word-final chandrakkala is not even silence — it is the **samvrutokaram**, a short central vowel that this pack’s own `ipa` column writes as `ɨ` on 436 cells, derived independently by espeak. Stripping it would delete a syllable rather than a spelling convention.

deviations.rule: Kannada’s undoing of Hindi’s four vowel-length collapses
deviations.why: Carried over unchanged. Malayalam writes all five length pairs with a dependent sign for both members — അ/ആ ഇ/ഈ ഉ/ഊ എ/ഏ ഒ/ഓ — so `policy.length` is `none` because the script carries the length and a bare `ː` has nothing left to do.

Absent, as in Telugu and Kannada. Malayalam has no nukta codepoint at all and writes loan /f/ as ഫ and loan /z/ as ജ — ഫോൺ, ഫോം, ജീറോ, ജോൺ. The cost is that /f/ collides with /pʰ/, which no Malayalam orthography can avoid.

approximations: Sounds with no Malayalam letter, and what they get. Malayalam’s own inventory is the largest of the four Dravidian scripts here — the whole four-way stop series, both retroflex and dental nasals, three sibilants, five vowel-length pairs, two phonemic rhotics and the retroflex approximant ഴ — so the list is shorter than Hindi’s or Kannada’s, and two of Kannada’s entries are replaced because they rest on a fact about *Kannada* usage. **`ɲ` is ഞ and not ന്യ**: Kannada’s ಞ appears in modern text essentially only inside the conjunct ಜ್ಞ, so its table spells the palatal nasal as a cluster — but Malayalam’s ഞ stands on its own in the commonest words in the language (ഞാൻ *I*, ഞങ്ങൾ *we*, ഞായറാഴ്ച *Sunday*), so Japanese に is ഞി and Spanish ñ is ഞ, both shapes a reader meets daily. **`ɻ` is ഴ**, Malayalam’s own letter for exactly that sound, where Kannada has none and gives it ರ. Otherwise: /ʔ/ and /ʕ/ are written as nothing, which leaves a Thai zero onset correctly bare. /ħ/ is ഹ. /θ ð/ are ഥ ദ, colliding with /t̪ d/ for the dental targets, which is the documented cost. /x ɣ q/ are ഖ ഗ ക. /ç/ is ഖ where the target has an /x/ for it to front (German ich) and ഹ where it does not (Japanese ひ). /y yː ʉ ø œ ɵ/ are ഊ/ൂ, Malayalam’s long u, which is how Malayalam print reads a front rounded vowel (മ്യൂണിക്, യൂറോ). /ɯ/ is ഉ, following the romanisation its two largest holders use — Japanese u and Korean ㅡ. /ɤ/ is ഏ, which is what Malayalam print gives Mandarin’s e. /ʎ/ is ല്യ, Hindi’s cluster shape kept because Malayalam has no palatal lateral. Bare /ŋ/ is ംഗ, the anusvara plus ഗ, which is exactly how Malayalam writes an English -ing: ബോർഡിംഗ്, റോമിംഗ്. Vietnamese’s glottalised codas and its /ˀ/ are dropped with the tone they belong to. /ʂ ʈʂ ʈʂʰ/ keep ഷ ച ഛ, since Malayalam ഷ is a live letter with its own retroflex value. Korean’s /ɰ/ and Mandarin’s /ɥ/ are വ and യ. Every rhotic — `r ɾ ɹ ʁ ʀ ɽ r̝ ʐ` — is ര, for the corpus reason the deviations record.
note:
**Malayalam is an abugida, so the design decision in this table is where the virama goes** — and Malayalam is the one Brahmic script here that has a second answer for half the cases. A consonant letter with nothing after it already says [a], so a cluster that forgets its chandrakkala does not merely look wrong: it prints a vowel the target does not have. Every consonant therefore has three spellings and `spellSlot`’s position decides between them: bare when it is the first thing in the syllable (`after_out: ""`), so a vowel sign can bind to it; virama-then-letter anywhere else in an onset, joining it to the consonant before; and letter-then-virama in a coda, killing its own inherent vowel.

**What Malayalam adds is the chillu, and it replaces the third of those three for five consonants.** ൺ ൻ ർ ൽ ൾ are single codepoints that mean "this consonant, no vowel", so a coda /n/ is ൻ rather than ന് — which is what modern Malayalam writes both word-finally (അവൻ, പാൽ, ആൾ) and before a consonant it does not fuse with (ആംബുലൻസ്, വർക്ക്). The remaining consonants keep the chandrakkala, and **a word-final chandrakkala in Malayalam is not silence**: it is the samvrutokaram, a very short central vowel, so ടിക്കറ്റ് is [ʈikkaʈʈɨ] and the column’s own `ɨ` and the romanisation’s `ŭ` are writing the same thing. A reader will therefore see a respelling one short vowel longer than the target word at the end of a consonant-final syllable, which is a property of the script rather than of this table.

**The conjuncts are ligatures with no codepoints of their own.** ക്ക, ന്ന, ണ്ട, ത്ത, ല്ല, ങ്ങ, ഞ്ഞ, മ്പ, ന്ത, സ്ഥ, ക്ഷ and the rest are reached only through GSUB from the same `C + ് + C` this table emits, which is why `MLYM_RANGES` in scripts/subset_fonts.py requests the block whole and `layout_features = ["*"]` is load-bearing. Which of the two orthographies prints — the traditional fused ligatures or the reformed detached signs — is decided by the shipped face and not by anything here; `mlym` is Manjari, which draws the traditional forms.

**A Malayalam consonant carries one vowel sign**, so a vowel in hiatus takes its independent letter — the 64 hiatus rules inherited from Telugu through Kannada, which found the defect on Vietnamese `biệt` and Ukrainian `hryvnia`. And **the bare-aspiration fallback is absent**: Hindi maps `ʰ` and `ʱ` to nothing, so an aspirate it has no rule for is silently spelt as its plain stop while `--gaps` reports nothing; every aspirate the corpus produces has a rule of its own here, with Malayalam’s own ഖ ഘ ഛ ഝ ഠ ഢ ഥ ധ ഫ ഭ. `ʲ`, `ˀ`, `ː` and `̃` keep their map-to-nothing rules, because those are *decisions*.
